intro: Four ways your senses and your brain decide what is out there. Run signal detection trials and move your criterion to trade hits against false alarms. Change a patch of light until you notice it and see Weber’s law. Stare at a flag and watch a real afterimage appear in the opponent colors. Then name the depth cues and Gestalt principles your brain uses to turn flat images into a world.
howItWorksTitle: About the models and the numbers
howItWorks:
Signal detection uses the standard textbook model: on each trial your sense of “something is there” is a normal curve, centered at 0 when there is only noise and further right when there is a signal (both with a standard deviation of 1). You say yes when it passes your criterion. The shaded areas are computed from the normal curve, so the percents are exact for the model; the trial dots are random draws from it.

Weber fractions are typical textbook values (about 8% for brightness, 2% for lifted weight); real fractions vary between people and conditions. The afterimage scene shows real colors: staring at the flag for 20 seconds and then at white gives most people an afterimage in the opponent colors. Data in the drills are invented for practice.
